The Name of the Rose. Umberto Eco's 1980 novel is a sophisticated mystery set in a medieval monastery where a series of seemingly unrelated deaths plague the community. The protagonist, a Franciscan friar and detective named William of Baskerville, must uncover the connection between the deaths and a secret hidden in the monastery's forbidden library, all while navigating theological disputes and political intrigue.

The setting is a fourteenth-century Benedictine monastery in northern Italy, isolated and bound by strict rules of silence and obedience. Deaths occur among the monks: poisonings, murders, and accidents that on the surface appear unconnected and possibly supernatural. William of Baskerville, a monk known for his powers of observation and deduction, arrives to investigate whether the deaths constitute a pattern.

As he works, William discovers that someone in the monastery is systematically murdering people to protect a secret text in the monastery's most forbidden wing. The mystery traces back to a book of Aristotle's lost writings on comedy. The church has suppressed this text because comedy is considered spiritually dangerous. William deduces that the killer is an elderly librarian who murders to keep the text hidden and preserve the church's control over knowledge and interpretation.

Eco's novel weaves detective mystery with philosophy, theology, semiotics, and political history, creating a layered narrative about truth and power. It challenges the conventions of detective fiction itself, blending literary theory with the intellectual substance of a genuine mystery.
